reason: The sources provide dozens of cross-verified facts across multiple independent domains confirming Enceladus's reflectivity, cryovolcanic plumes, subsurface ocean, and ring creation.
story: Saturn's tiny moon Enceladus is only about 310 miles wide, yet it is the most reflective body in the entire Solar System. Blanketed in pristine snow, it bounces back almost all incoming sunlight, keeping surface temperatures at a bone-chilling minus 324 degrees Fahrenheit. For decades after William Herschel discovered it in 1789, scientists wondered why this frozen speck stayed so dazzlingly bright. In 2005, NASA's Cassini spacecraft solved the mystery. Massive geysers near the south pole erupt from fractures called tiger stripes, shooting water vapor, salts, and organic molecules hundreds of miles into space. While much of this icy spray falls back to coat the moon in fresh snow, the rest escapes into orbit, building Saturn's massive E ring from scratch. By tracking the moon's subtle orbital wobble, scientists proved these jets tap directly into a global liquid ocean hidden beneath miles of ice.
angle: Saturn's moon Enceladus is an active cryovolcanic engine that blasts its own global ocean into space, simultaneously repainting itself blinding white and building Saturn's entire E ring.

claims.claim: William Herschel discovered Enceladus on August 28, 1789.
Enceladus was named after a giant from Greek mythology by John Herschel in an 1847 publication.
Enceladus is approximately 500 kilometers (310 miles) in diameter.
Enceladus is the most reflective body in the Solar System.
Because Enceladus reflects so much sunlight, its surface temperature reaches around minus 198 to minus 201 degrees Celsius (minus 324 to minus 330 degrees Fahrenheit).
Enceladus orbits Saturn at a distance of about 238,000 kilometers (148,000 miles) between Mimas and Tethys.
Enceladus completes one orbit around Saturn every 32.9 hours and keeps the same face toward the planet.
Enceladus is trapped in an orbital resonance with Dione, completing two orbits for every one orbit of Dione.
Gravitational interactions cause tidal heating within Enceladus.
In 2005, the Cassini spacecraft discovered water vapor and icy plumes erupting from Enceladus's south polar region.
The eruptions emanate from fractures in the crust informally dubbed 'tiger stripes'.
Eruptions from Enceladus supply the material that forms Saturn's E ring.
Material falling back to the surface as snow maintains Enceladus's bright white appearance.
The plumes contain salts and organic molecules.
Cassini detected silica particles in the plume, indicating hydrothermal reactions between liquid water and rock.
Measurements of Enceladus's rotational wobble, or libration, proved that a global liquid ocean separates the icy crust from the rocky core.
Models based on libration measurements estimate Enceladus's global ocean is 26 to 31 kilometers deep, compared to Earth's average ocean depth of 3.7 kilometers.
Gravity data from Cassini flybys detected mass anomalies indicating dense liquid water beneath an ice shell.

disputed: Regional sea vs. global ocean: Early Cassini gravity analyses in 2014 suggested a localized sea under the south pole, whereas 2015 libration measurements confirmed the ocean is moon-wide; scripts should present the global ocean as the finalized discovery.

Proportion of plume material escaping into the E ring: S1 states that some falls back and the rest supplies most of the E ring material, while S2 specifies only a small fraction escapes into the ring while most falls back as snow; scripts should avoid rigid percentages and say part escapes to build the ring while much falls back as snow.

Ice shell thickness: S3 and S5 cite an ice shell 30 to 40 km thick, while S2 cites an average global thickness of 20 to 25 km and as thin as 1 to 5 km at the south pole; scripts should specify that thickness estimates vary across regions.
